name: Sivatherium
fact: The biggest giraffe that ever lived — much bigger than today's giraffes! It had elaborate head ornaments like a cross between a giraffe and a moose. It survived until humans arrived in its territory.

name: Macrauchenia
fact: A weird South American mammal with a trunk-like upper lip! Related to llamas and camels but looking nothing like them. It survived until humans hunted it to extinction a few thousand years ago.
sites: Puerto San Julián — found by Darwin, 1834

name: Chalicothere
fact: A giant mammal with horse-like body but CLAWS instead of hooves! Used them to pull down branches. An evolutionary experiment that lasted millions of years but couldn't compete once horses dominated.

name: Megalodon
habitat: Warm coastal and open oceans worldwide
fact: The largest shark and one of the largest fish ever to live - bigger than a school bus with teeth the size of a human hand. Megalodon specialized in hunting large whales. It went extinct approximately 3.6 million years ago, likely due to cooling oceans and the decline of its prey.
know: Shark skeletons are cartilage, which rarely fossilises, so megalodon is known almost entirely from teeth up to 18 cm long and a few backbones. Every size you have seen quoted is an estimate scaled from those.
debate: How long, and what shape? Estimates run from 15 to over 20 m, and a 2025 study argued for a longer, slimmer body than the giant great white of the films.

name: Deinotherium
fact: A giant elephant relative with downward-curving tusks on the lower jaw - the opposite direction from all other proboscideans. Dinotherium used these tusks to strip bark from trees. It persisted for an extraordinary 19 million years, one of the longest-lived large mammal genera ever.

name: Hipparion
fact: A three-toed horse that spread from North America across land bridges to populate every continent except Australia and Antarctica. Hipparion was so successful that its fossils are used worldwide as a marker for Miocene grassland deposits.

name: Ekembo (Proconsul)
fact: An early ape: it walked along branches on all fours like a monkey — but it had no tail. Every ape since, including you, is tailless.
know: Volcanic ash on Rusinga Island in Lake Victoria buried and preserved whole skeletons. The first skull was found by Mary Leakey in 1948.

name: Platybelodon
fact: A “shovel-tusker”: an elephant relative whose lower jaw ended in two broad, flat tusks side by side.
know: It was long drawn scooping up water plants. Scratch patterns on the tusks tell a different story: it used them like a scythe, gripping branches with its trunk and sawing them off.

name: Phorusrhacos (Terror Bird)
fact: A flightless, fast-running bird with a hooked beak the size of a horse's head. With no big cats or wolves in island South America, giant birds were among the top predators for tens of millions of years.

name: Sivapithecus
fact: An ape from the foothills of the Himalayas with a face strikingly like an orangutan's — a member of the Asian branch of the great-ape family.
know: In the 1960s its thick-enamelled teeth led some to call it a human ancestor 14 million years old. A face found in Pakistan in 1979, and DNA evidence that humans and chimps split far more recently, settled it: orangutan line, not ours.

name: Danuvius
means: After the Celtic river-god of the Danube
fact: An ape from Bavaria, described in 2019, with long hanging arms — and leg bones that suggest it could stand with straight knees on branches.
debate: Its discoverers argue that upright posture began in the trees of Europe, long before our line left the forest. Others reply that the bones are too incomplete, and too crushed, to say how it moved.

name: Livyatan
means: Leviathan — its species name honours Herman Melville
fact: A sperm whale that hunted other whales. Its teeth, up to 36 cm long, are the largest biting teeth of any animal known — and it shared the sea with the giant shark megalodon.

name: Thylacosmilus
fact: It looks like a sabre-toothed cat. It is not a cat, or even close: it is a relative of marsupials that evolved the same weapon independently in South America.
know: The same solution appearing in unrelated animals — sabre teeth, wings, streamlined swimmers — is called convergent evolution, and it is some of the best evidence that natural selection shapes bodies to their way of life.

name: Amphicyon
fact: A “bear-dog” — neither bear nor dog, but a separate family that had features of both.

name: Teleoceras
fact: A short-legged, hippo-like rhino. At Ashfall, Nebraska, over 100 died around a waterhole after a volcanic ashfall — some calves still beside their mothers.

name: Merychippus
fact: The first grazing horse, with tall teeth to grind gritty grass. It still had three toes, but walked on the middle one.

name: Aepycamelus
size: About 3 m tall at the head
fact: A “giraffe camel” with very long legs and neck, browsing on treetops in North America.

name: Gomphotherium
fact: An elephant relative with four tusks — two up, two in the lower jaw. Its family spread to every continent except Australia and Antarctica.

name: Anancus
fact: An elephant relative with straight tusks up to 4 m long — almost as long as its body.

name: Argentavis
fact: The largest flying bird known — a giant soaring relative of condors, using the wind off the Andes to stay aloft.

name: Kelenken
fact: A terror bird with the largest skull of any bird known — 71 cm long, mostly hooked beak.

name: Pelagornis
fact: A seabird with tooth-like spikes of bone along its beak and the longest wings of any bird. It glided over the oceans like an albatross.

name: Puijila
fact: A walking seal: an otter-like animal with webbed feet, from the Canadian Arctic. It shows seals came from land carnivores.

name: Odobenocetops
fact: A whale relative with a walrus-like face and one very long tusk. It probably sucked clams off the seabed.

name: Megantereon
fact: A sabre-toothed cat of Africa and Eurasia. It lived alongside early humans at Dmanisi, Georgia.

name: Agriotherium
fact: A giant short-faced bear that ranged from Europe and Africa to North America.

name: Samotherium
fact: A giraffe relative with a neck halfway between an okapi's and a giraffe's — a step in how the giraffe's neck stretched.

name: Stupendemys
fact: One of the largest turtles ever, with a shell longer than a person is tall. Males had horns on the front of their shells — probably for fighting each other.

name: Purussaurus
fact: A giant caiman — one of the largest crocodilians ever, top predator of the swamps where the Amazon once drained north.

name: Synthetoceras
fact: Males carried a long horn on the nose that split into a Y at the tip, like a catapult — plus another pair over the eyes.

name: Prolibytherium
fact: A giraffe relative whose horns grew into a single flat, leaf-shaped plate spread across its head, like a pair of butterfly wings.

name: Astrapotherium
fact: A big South American plant-eater with tusks, a short trunk and a body like a tapir crossed with a hippo — from an order of mammals with no living members.

name: Thalassocnus
fact: A sloth that went to sea. On the desert coast of Peru, ground sloths waded out to graze seagrass — and over five species, across millions of years, became better and better swimmers.
know: The younger the species, the denser its bones (ballast for diving) and the more worn its teeth from sandy seagrass — evolution recorded layer by layer.

name: Desmostylus
habitat: Coastal shallows of the North Pacific
fact: A hippo-like sea mammal from an order that is completely extinct. Its teeth look like bundles of pencils standing on end — no living animal has anything similar.
debate: What did it eat, and how did it move? Seaweed or seagrass; walking like a hippo or swimming like a polar bear — every reconstruction looks different.

name: Simbakubwa
size: Possibly heavier than a polar bear
fact: A giant hyaenodont meat-eater — not a cat, despite its name — with a head bigger than a lion's. It was found in a museum drawer in Nairobi decades after it was dug up.

name: Barbourofelis
fact: It had some of the longest sabre teeth of any animal — so long that its lower jaw grew a bony flange like a sheath to protect them.

name: Ekaltadeta
fact: The “killer kangaroo”: a relative of kangaroos with big, blade-like slicing teeth at the front of its mouth.
debate: Did it actually hunt? The teeth could slice meat — or tough fruit and fungi. Most think it ate both.

name: Yalkparidon
size: Small — known from skulls and teeth
fact: Nicknamed “Thingodonta”, because its teeth look like those of no other mammal ever found. Nobody knows what it ate or who its relatives were.

name: Nimbadon
fact: A sheep-sized relative of wombats that climbed trees, gripping with big curved claws.
know: A cave opening hidden in the forest floor trapped a whole group — from babies in the pouch to adults — so scientists could follow how it grew.

name: Obdurodon
fact: A platypus with teeth. Baby platypuses today grow teeth and then lose them; Obdurodon kept its teeth all its life.

name: Dromornis
size: About 3 m tall, up to 600 kg
fact: One of the heaviest birds that ever lived. Despite looking like a giant emu, it belonged to the family of ducks and geese.

name: Bullockornis
fact: Nicknamed the “demon duck of doom”: a giant flightless relative of ducks with a huge, deep beak.
debate: Was the beak for crushing meat and bone, or tough seeds and fruit? Scans of its brain and skull have pointed both ways.

name: Titanis
fact: The only terror bird known from North America. It walked north from South America when the two continents joined.
know: It was once thought to have survived until 15,000 years ago. New dating of its rocks showed it was far older.

name: Mourasuchus
fact: A caiman with a long, flat, duck-like snout and weak jaws. It probably gulped mouthfuls of water and filtered out small fish — a giant crocodile that ate like a pelican.

name: Oreopithecus
fact: An island ape from Tuscany and Sardinia, where there were no big predators.
debate: Its hands suggest a precise grip and its hips have been read as built for some upright walking — evolved on an island, independently of our own line. Other researchers find no sign of upright walking at all.

name: Palaeocastor
fact: A small beaver that lived on dry land and dug spiral burrows over 2 m deep.
know: The fossil corkscrews were called “Daemonelix” — devil's corkscrews — and argued over for years: giant sponges? Plant roots? Then a beaver skeleton was found curled at the bottom of one.

name: Ceratogaulus
fact: The horned gopher: the only rodent ever known to have horns — a pair on its nose.
debate: Horns for digging, for display, or for fending off predators? Females had them too, which makes display less likely.

name: Josephoartigasia
size: About 3 m long, perhaps half a tonne
fact: The largest rodent known — a relative of the living pacarana the size of a bull, with incisors it may have used like tusks.
debate: Weight estimates have ranged from about 500 kg to over a tonne — it is known from just one skull.

name: Deinogalerix
fact: A hedgehog relative the size of a cat, with no spines — just coarse hair and a long snout. It lived on Gargano, then an island, where animals evolved in odd directions.

name: Hoplitomeryx
size: About 50 cm–1 m at the shoulder
fact: A deer-like island animal with five horns — one in the middle of its forehead — and long, sabre-like upper canine teeth.

name: Chapalmalania
fact: A raccoon relative the size of a bear. Its ancestors crossed from North to South America by island-hopping, before the land bridge existed.

name: Nyanzapithecus (“Alesi”)
fact: The skull of a baby ape about 16 months old, buried by a volcano 13 million years ago and nicknamed Alesi — “ancestor” in the Turkana language. X-rays of its inner ear show it was not a fast, swinging climber like a gibbon.
know: The skull is about the size of a lemon. Its unerupted adult teeth, still inside the jaw, were imaged with X-rays at a synchrotron in France; their growth lines gave its age.

name: Phoberomys
fact: A rodent the size of a buffalo, living by the rivers of what is now Venezuela. Its estimated weight is more than ten times a capybara’s, the biggest rodent alive.

name: Arctic camel (Paracamelus)
size: About a third bigger than a living camel
habitat: Arctic forest of larch and birch
fact: A giant camel living in a forest on Ellesmere Island, about 1,200 km from the North Pole, in the warm Pliocene. Camels began in North America; this one shows some lived in the far north before they crossed to Asia.
know: It is known from 30 pieces of one leg bone. Proteins still inside the bone matched those of camels.

name: Protarctos
size: Known from a skull and teeth
habitat: Arctic forest by a beaver pond
fact: An early relative of today’s black and brown bears, from the forests of the High Arctic. Its teeth have cavities — a sign of a sweet diet, probably berries, perhaps eaten to fatten up for a long winter.

name: Chasmaporthetes (running hyena)
fact: A long-legged hyena built for running prey down. It is the only hyena known to have reached the Americas, crossing from Asia; two teeth found at Old Crow in the Yukon show the way it came.

name: Wakaleo
size: About the size of a dog
fact: A marsupial lion of Australia’s Miocene forests, with slicing teeth and strong climbing arms — an earlier, smaller relative of Thylacoleo.

name: Lufengpithecus
fact: An ape of southern China known from hundreds of teeth and several skulls, living while the first members of the human family were appearing in Africa.

name: Dinofelis
fact: A jaguar-sized cat with teeth halfway between a lion’s and a sabre-tooth’s. Its bones lie in the same South African caves as our early relatives — who may well have been its prey.

name: Stegodon
size: Up to about 4 m at the shoulder
fact: An elephant cousin whose long tusks grew so close together that its trunk had to hang to one side. Dwarf kinds lived on Indonesian islands, where the “hobbits” of Flores hunted them.
